title: How to Deal With Company Politics as an Engineering Leader
author: Ojstersek, Gregor
summary: Drawing on 13-plus years in engineering, this piece is a practical field guide for newly promoted engineering managers who discover, often abruptly, that the job is far less about code and far more about navigating people and politics. The author illustrates the shock with his own story: witnessing executives publicly blame each other in a meeting, and later being formally reported to his own manager for trying to improve a process outside his direct team's remit, purely for stepping outside his 'lane.' His core thesis is that the best idea rarely wins on its own merits inside an organization — what actually determines whether change happens is relationships, reputation, credibility, and the ability to influence, and he offers five concrete moves to build these deliberately: learn how senior peers prefer to work before pushing new processes on them, map the informal 'influence diagram' (which is not the same as the org chart), invest in relationships proactively, build credibility and social proof through visible work like writing and speaking, and consciously avoid unhealthy political behaviors (public blame, urgency theater, being 'always online') just because a leader models them. The piece ends with a sober, non-heroic conclusion: since company politics rarely change without a shift at the top (starting with the CEO), the honest question every leader eventually needs to ask isn't how to fix a toxic environment but whether it's healthy enough to stay in long-term.
points: Names the exact shock of first-time management: the job stops being about engineering and becomes almost entirely about navigating people and organizational politics.
Distinguishes the real 'influence diagram' (who actually has sway) from the formal reporting chart — arguing decisions get made through the former, not the latter.

Gives a specific, actionable checklist: learn peers' working styles first, build relationships deliberately, invest in visible credibility (writing, speaking), and consciously avoid modeling unhealthy political behaviors just because leaders above you do.
Ends with an unusually candid admission for a leadership newsletter: company politics rarely change without a shift at the CEO level, so sometimes the right answer is to leave, not fix it.
quotes: A new engineer gets promoted and becomes a manager for the first time. That new engineer quite quickly discovers that the new role is less about engineering and a lot more about dealing with people.
What I quickly found out is that the best solution doesn't always win... In some cases, I was even reported to my manager for trying to 'stick my nose into something that's none of my business.'
What I quickly learned is that good relationships, your reputation, and credibility + being able to influence well, that's what's really important in order to manoeuvre company politics well.
This is crucial because that's how you're going to better understand how decisions get made, and the influence diagram is not always the same as the reporting diagram.

Company politics rarely change unless there is a drastic change in leadership, starting with the CEO. So, always ask yourself this question: 'Is this environment healthy for me to be a part of long-term or not?'
